There are hands in this world that can read the grain of granite like a love letter, and with a touch, know exactly where the stone wants to break. The same hands can place a block weighing more than a family of mammoths within a hair’s breadth of its neighbor, no mortar needed, and know it will hold for ten thousand years. And then, those same four-clawed hands can leave the quarry for the forge, and beat a truth out of bronze that other smiths will spend a lifetime chasing.
These are the hands of the Barran Orves.

When you picture them, don’t picture their taller, sea-wandering cousins, the Albans. The Barran Orves are built for the mountains that made them. Shorter, wider, with a center of gravity so low to the ground they seem a part of the bedrock itself. They are dense with muscle, thick of limb, born with a stability that serves them as well on a high ledge as it does at the anvil. They evolved in the thin, cold air of the Tibetan plateau and the Altai mountains, and their bodies are furnaces, built to burn hot and work hard where the air is unforgiving.

They also have time. A Barran Orve can live for nearly two centuries. Think of what that means for a craft. Mastery isn’t the work of one lifetime; it’s the work of one very, very long one. A smith of one hundred and twenty years has a century of muscle memory in their arms, a century of fire-gazing in their eyes. For them, patience isn’t a virtue; it’s a simple fact of life. They have the decades to give.

They were the first to master bronze, a quarter of a million years ago. It happened because they lived where the ore was, and they already knew the secrets of fire. But what they built with that discovery was more than a technology. It was a philosophy. To a Barran Orve, the quality of an object is a moral statement. A shoddy tool is not just a failure of craft; it’s a failure of character. A perfectly balanced blade is not just a weapon; it is an argument for honor, forged and tempered into steel.

This is where they part ways with their Alban kin. The Albans believe knowledge lives in the mind, passed from one generation to the next in story and song. If the singer dies, the song is lost. But the Barrans… they encode their knowledge into the thing itself. The formula for an alloy lives in the crystalline structure of the axe-head. The principles of architecture live in the earthquake-proof walls of the chamber. Their knowledge has a physical body. After the world breaks, an Alban’s knowledge survives only if the person survives. A Barran’s knowledge survives in the rooms they built, waiting in the dark to be read again.

You might think a people so tied to the forge and the quarry would stay in one place. But they are also some of the world's great nomads. It’s a contradiction that works perfectly for them. The forge-settlement, their deep home, stays. It is the heart, the anchor, tended by generations of craftspeople. But the clans move. They are the first and the greatest horsemen, their caravans a constant presence on the trade routes of the vast central steppe, carrying metals and tools to the corners of the world. They wander far, but they are never rootless. They are a people with a permanent home they can leave whenever they wish.

And their homes are not what they seem. What you see on the surface—the workshops, the markets—is just the welcome hall. The true city is below. The Barran Orves have been building down for longer than Atlantis has been a name. Deep, deep into the rock, they carve out libraries. Not of scrolls or skins, but of stone. Chambers with walls inscribed floor to ceiling with metallurgical equations, star charts, histories, the genealogies of clans. They built a world under the world, designed to outlast anything the sky might throw at it.

They are a quiet people. They measure worth in skill, not speeches. You don't tell someone you're a master smith; you show them a blade that sings when it’s drawn. A boaster is seen as a fool, someone wasting the breath and time that could be spent making something true. Loyalty is to the clan, first and always. A debt to one is a debt to all; an insult to one is an insult that the entire family will remember for a century. Honor, to them, is simple: it is proven competence. It is the ability to do. Everything else is just noise.

This, of course, makes their relationship with the eloquent, wandering Alban Orves a complicated one. It is the oldest partnership in the world. For ages beyond counting, the Albans have brought their sea-charts and coastal goods to the Barrans, and the Barrans have sent them home with the finest tools and weapons metal can make. They rely on each other utterly. And they irritate each other profoundly. The Albans think the Barrans are stubborn as rock and far too secretive, burying their truth in the dark. The Barrans think the Alban way of keeping knowledge—in fragile memories and records that rot—is a kind of foolish arrogance. A blade you refuse to temper. The friction is, I think, part of what makes the bond so strong.

When the great catastrophe came, all those little disagreements vanished. What mattered was that they were kin. What mattered was that the deepest, safest places in the world had been built by Barran hands. In Anatolia, in the region we now call Cappadocia, there are ancient cities underground. Our own explorers have mapped levels reaching eighty-five meters down. They call it Derinkuyu. But what they’ve found is only the lobby. The upper floors. The deeper levels, the great libraries of stone, have not been opened. Not yet.

The Barran Orves are gone from the surface of the world. But they are not gone from our stories. We remember them without knowing their names. Every myth of the Dwarf—the master smith who lives inside the mountain, grumpy and brilliant, who forges the treasures of the gods—that is the echo of a Barran Orve. The Greek god Hephaestus, the lame craftsman working his volcanic forge, whose worth is entirely in his hands… that is a memory of them.

Their mastery of the horse was so complete, so alien to those who saw it for the first time, that the memory warped. Over thousands of years, the image of a stocky, bearded rider and his powerful mount blurred into one being: the Centaur.

And there is one last trace, quieter and more real than any myth. In the mountains of Tibet today, there are people who carry genes for high-altitude adaptation that are found nowhere else. Genes that let them breathe the thin air that would kill another person. That is not a story. That is a legacy, written in blood and bone. The Barran Orves are gone. But their breath is still in us.
